data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for corroborated theories smuggles induction back into Popper's system, rendering his rejection of probabilistic confirmation inconsistent with scientific practice.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a non-inductive justification for action (e.g., game-theoretic or evolutionary) can be rigorously demonstrated.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference is framed purely as a psychological necessity rather than a rational norm.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's distinction between 'acceptance for testing' and 'acceptance for action' holds up under scrutiny.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"To prefer Theory A over Theory B solely because A has survived tests that B has not (or A has survived more severe tests) logically presupposes that past performance is a reliable guide to future performance. This is the very definition of the problem of induction. If the future is not assumed to resemble the past, the fact that a theory worked yesterday provides zero logical warrant for expecting it to work tomorrow. By advising scientists to 'act' on the best-tested theory, Popper implicitly accepts an inductive principle: that corroboration indicates a higher propensity for future success, which is functionally identical to assigning it a higher probability, contradicting his core thesis.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
